title: CredibleDFGO: Differentiable Factor Graph Optimization with Credibility Supervision
subjects: Signal Processing (eess.SP); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Submitted to NAVIGATION: Journal of the Institute of Navigation
abstract: [Abstract]Global navigation satellite system (GNSS) positioning is widely used for urban navigation, but the covariance reported by the GNSS solver is often unreliable in urban canyons. Existing differentiable factor graph optimization (DFGO) methods already learn measurement weighting through the solver, but they still use position-only objectives. As a result, the mean estimate may improve while the reported covariance remains too small, too large, or wrong in shape. In this work, we propose CredibleDFGO (CDFGO), a differentiable GNSS factor graph framework that makes covariance credibility an explicit training target. The Weighting Generation Network (WGN) predicts per-satellite reliability weights. The differentiable Gauss–Newton solver maps these weights to a position estimate and posterior covariance, and proper scoring rules supervise the East–North predictive distribution end-to-end. We study negative log-likelihood (NLL), Energy Score (ES), and their combination. Results on three UrbanNav test scenes show consistent gains in uncertainty credibility. Positioning accuracy also improves on the medium-urban and harsh-urban scenes, and the mean horizontal error and 95th-percentile error improve on the deep-urban scene. On the harsh-urban Mong Kok (MK) scene, CDFGO-Combined reduces the mean horizontal error from 13.77 m to 11.68 m, reduces NLL from 40.63 to 6.59, and reduces ES from 12.31 to 9.05. The case studies link the MK improvement to better axis-wise consistency, more credible local covariance ellipses, and satellite-level reweighting.
introduction:
GNSS positioning in urban canyons can return an accurate position, but the reported covariance does not match the true position error. This mismatch matters because the covariance is not just a diagnostic number. It directly controls downstream decisions. The covariance controls how much fusion modules trust the GNSS position update and when integrity monitors raise an alert. A miscalibrated covariance misleads both. Li and colleagues gave this problem a name: credibility [23]. Credibility assesses whether the reported uncertainty is statistically consistent with the true position error. Position accuracy alone does not tell us whether the reported uncertainty was credible. Yan and colleagues recently showed that two proper scoring rules, negative log-likelihood (NLL) and the energy score (ES), can detect different kinds of covariance miscalibration in state estimators under noise and model mismatch [48]. These different kinds of miscalibration correspond to three concrete failure modes. The reported ellipse may be too small, too large, or pointing in the wrong direction. In horizontal positioning, a tight ellipse can still fail to cover the true East–North position. Two downstream systems show why this risk is not just theoretical. Joerger and Pervan showed that sequential advanced receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (ARAIM) can exploit satellite motion over time only when the uncertainty model stays credible [13]. In driverless urban navigation, Nagai and colleagues found that fault-free integrity requires credible GNSS uncertainty for fusion with other onboard sensors [28]. Therefore, credibility cannot be inferred from the position error. It must be assessed directly from the reported covariance. This requirement applies to any estimator family — classical weighted least squares, robust filters, or learned factor graphs.

Yet most work in urban GNSS targets position accuracy, not covariance credibility. Most methods work on the measurements before they reach the solver. Zheng and colleagues predicted satellite visibility from a sky-plot graph using a graph transformer [51]. Building on 3D city models, Wang and colleagues distinguished LOS from NLOS signals using shadow matching [38]. Ng and colleagues also extended 3D-mapping-aided GNSS to dual-frequency smartphone pseudoranges [29]. Li and colleagues learned NLOS-aware weights from signal features, so contaminated and clean measurements are weighted differently [22]. Mohanty and Gao used graph convolutions to learn smartphone GNSS corrections from inter-satellite relations [26]. Smolyakov and colleagues adapted the stochastic model online through multipath prediction and detection [34]. A more direct approach by Chen and colleagues learned pseudorange corrections that reduce urban bias directly [2]. Kanhere and colleagues trained a set transformer to predict position corrections from pseudorange residuals and line-of-sight vectors [15]. Zhang and colleagues took a different direction by making measurement uncertainty itself the prediction target, using an LSTM to model its time-varying behavior [50]. Medina and colleagues reviewed classical robust GNSS estimators under harsh conditions, showing that standard least squares becomes unreliable when outliers and heavy tails dominate [25]. Even a dedicated urban M-estimator was found to be sensitive to the choice of the error model, and its performance depended on proper design [6]. Li and colleagues tuned the Huber M-estimator parameters using the logistic distribution of GNSS errors, reducing the 2D RMSE and suppressing large error spikes [24]. Yan and colleagues isolated multi-constellation faults through incremental expansion of a fault-free basic set [46]. All of these methods target the measurements or the robust estimator before the solver runs. The covariance the solver returns is never their supervision target.

The same gap exists within the factor‑graph framework. Several methods address measurement faults and integrity monitoring, but they still do not supervise the covariance. Wen, Hsu, and colleagues brought factor-graph optimization into robust GNSS and RTK positioning [40]. They later applied graduated non-convexity to downweight pseudorange outliers [42], and a related thread from the same group fused GNSS and LiDAR with self-adaptive Gaussian mixtures [39]. Yan and colleagues learned subspace-based adaptive GMM error models for fault-aware urban positioning [47]. Knowles and Gao developed rapid fault detection and exclusion [19]. For long-term integrity, Gallon and colleagues hardened orbit and clock error modeling [5]. Xia and colleagues came closest to the covariance credibility question. Their integrity-constrained factor graph uses switch variables to reweight measurements and derives a protection level from the modified weighting matrix, though their method does not involve learning [43]. Their work shows that the factor-graph framework can engage with covariance, but it needs a training signal that targets it. Without such a signal, even general-purpose uncertainty quantification tools face the same limitation. Gal and Ghahramani’s Monte Carlo dropout approximates Bayesian uncertainty by sampling subnetworks, but the factor-graph solver already provides a posterior covariance from the inverse of the converged Hessian [4]. Levi and colleagues showed how to calibrate regression uncertainty after training, but post-hoc calibration does not change which satellites receive high weight during the forward pass [21]. None of these approaches train the covariance to match the true position error.

A different route is needed to supervise the covariance. In a differentiable factor graph, the solver is unrolled so that gradients flow from the loss back through the optimization to the factor weights. Because the posterior covariance is produced by the Hessian of the converged solution, a credibility loss can directly penalize a miscalibrated covariance through the same backward pass.

This idea builds on decades of work on factor graphs for robot perception. Dellaert and Kaess formulated factor graphs and smoothing as a sparse probabilistic framework that incorporates measurements, priors, and constraints inside one optimization problem [3]. The iSAM2 and Bayes tree formulations from Kaess and colleagues made incremental smoothing practical at navigation scale [14], and Taylor and Gross recently framed the whole family as a navigation generalization of Kalman filtering for systems that mix asynchronous sensors [35]. Several groups have also tried to embed learning inside GNSS estimators. Mohanty and Gao connected a graph neural network to a backpropagation Kalman filter so that the learned corrections directly affect the state estimate [27]. Hu and colleagues coupled deep bias and weight prediction with RTKLIB-style positioning [12]. In these designs, the learning signal reaches the estimator output and gradients flow through the estimator. However, the training loss still targets only the position estimate. Mohanty and Gao note explicitly that they leave covariance learning for future work. These designs make the estimator differentiable but do not unroll the factor graph optimization itself. Yi and colleagues addressed this by unrolling the optimization steps and backpropagating through them [49], establishing DFGO as a training paradigm. The idea of differentiating through a solved optimization problem is not limited to navigation. Amos and Kolter treated optimization as a neural-network layer in OptNet and derived exact gradients through solved programs [1]. Xu and colleagues’ DFGO-ICov brought this idea to smartphone GNSS, with a network predicting adaptive covariance scales for pseudorange factors and a differentiable solver training these scales against ground-truth position [45]. Their follow-up AutoW replaced ground-truth labels with self-supervised priors from clustering and zero-velocity constraints, reporting gains over classical weighting schemes [44]. But the training loss in these methods still acts on the position estimate, not the posterior covariance. A position-only loss cannot distinguish a covariance that is tight and correct from one that is tight but misoriented, because both can yield the same position estimate.

A loss that only sees the position error cannot judge whether the covariance is right. To evaluate both the position estimate and the posterior covariance, the loss must act on the full predictive distribution that the solver outputs. Proper scoring rules do exactly this. A strictly proper scoring rule attains its lowest expected value only when the predicted distribution matches the true distribution. This means a covariance that looks precise but is poorly calibrated is penalized, not rewarded. For the two-dimensional East–North prediction, scoring each axis independently fails to capture the correlation between the two axes [7, 8, 33]. Yan and colleagues already used these scoring rules as credibility metrics for state estimators [48]. CDFGO uses the same rules and turns them into training losses inside a differentiable solver. For the East–North Gaussian predictor used in GNSS, NLL penalizes a position estimate that is far from the true position and a covariance ellipse that is too small, too large, or pointing in the wrong direction. The energy score works differently: it measures the expected distance from predictive samples to the true position, minus half the expected distance between pairs of predictive samples. Because the energy score does not assume that the errors follow a Gaussian distribution, it remains informative when the urban pseudorange errors are heavy-tailed. Under a credible Gaussian predictor, about 68% of axis-wise errors should lie within the reported 1-σ\sigma bound and about 99.7% within the 3-σ\sigma bound. CredibleDFGO (CDFGO) implements this credibility supervision end-to-end. A Weighting Generation Network (WGN) maps per-satellite features to reliability weights, which a differentiable Gauss–Newton solver [30] uses as per-factor information weights, and the gradients flow directly through the solver back to the WGN parameters [1]. We study three variants. CDFGO-NLL optimizes the Gaussian NLL of the East–North posterior, CDFGO-ES optimizes the energy score, and CDFGO-Combined trains against both. We evaluate CDFGO on three UrbanNav test scenes covering medium-urban, deep-urban, and harsh-urban conditions. Credibility-driven weighting can suppress contaminated satellites that still contribute to the geometry, so this sometimes results in weaker geometry that yields a covariance that better matches the true position error. This geometry-credibility tradeoff is a core feature of the method, not a side effect.

The contributions of this paper are threefold:

We show that proper scoring rules, when used as end-to-end training losses for a differentiable GNSS factor graph, make the posterior covariance a supervised output rather than an unsupervised byproduct.

We develop the CredibleDFGO framework and demonstrate on three UrbanNav scenes that credibility-driven training improves uncertainty credibility while preserving or improving horizontal accuracy.

We identify a geometry-credibility tradeoff inherent in credibility-driven weighting. A satellite-level analysis on the Mong Kok scene shows how this tradeoff reshapes the posterior covariance and why it still improves both accuracy and credibility.

1. We show that proper scoring rules, when used as end-to-end training losses for a differentiable GNSS factor graph, make the posterior covariance a supervised output rather than an unsupervised byproduct.

2. We develop the CredibleDFGO framework and demonstrate on three UrbanNav scenes that credibility-driven training improves uncertainty credibility while preserving or improving horizontal accuracy.

3. We identify a geometry-credibility tradeoff inherent in credibility-driven weighting. A satellite-level analysis on the Mong Kok scene shows how this tradeoff reshapes the posterior covariance and why it still improves both accuracy and credibility.

title: Leveraging Image Generators to Address Training Data Scarcity: The Gen4Regen Dataset for Forest Regeneration Mapping
authors: Gabriel Jeanson,David-Alexandre Duclos,William Larrivée-Hardy,Noé Cochet,Matěj Boxan,Anthony Deschênes,François Pomerleau,Philippe Giguère
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Sustainable forest management relies on precise species composition mapping, yet traditional ground surveys are labour-intensive and geographically constrained.
While Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles offer scalable data collection, the transition to deep learning-based interpretation is bottlenecked by the severe scarcity of expert-annotated imagery, particularly in complex, visually heterogeneous regeneration zones.
This paper addresses the dual challenges of data scarcity and extreme class imbalance in the semantic segmentation of fine-grained forest regeneration species by providing a scalable framework that reduces reliance on manual photo-interpretation for high-resolution, millimetre-level aerial imagery.
Importantly, we leverage the large-scale vision-language Nano Banana Pro model to simultaneously generate high-fidelity images and their corresponding pixel-aligned semantic masks from prompts.
We introduce WilDReF-Q-V2, an expansion of a natural forest dataset with 13 97713\,977 new unlabelled and 5050 labelled real images, as well as the Gen4Regen dataset, featuring 21012101 pairs of synthetic images and semantic masks.
Our methodology integrates real-world data with AI-generated images, addressing both data scarcity and class imbalance in forest regeneration mapping.
We evaluate the orthogonality of manual labels, automated pseudo-labels, and synthetic data using Mask2Former and DINOv2 architectures, highlighting that AI-generated data is highly complementary to real-world pseudo-labels, with unified training yielding an F1 score improvement of over 15 %pt15\text{\,}\mathrm{\%pt} compared to purely supervised baselines.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that even small quantities of prompt-generated data significantly improve performance for underrepresented species, some of which saw per-species F1 score gains of up to 30 %pt30\text{\,}\mathrm{\%pt}.
We conclude that vision-language models can serve as agile data generators, effectively bootstrapping perception tasks for niche AI domains where expert labels are scarce or unavailable.
This paradigm enables practitioners to bypass seasonal data collection constraints and develop specialized ecological monitoring systems with minimal manual effort.
Our datasets, source code, and models will be available at https://norlab-ulaval.github.io/gen4regen.
introduction:
Forest regeneration is critical for sustainable land management and biodiversity conservation, particularly following disturbances such as wildfire, disease, or logging.
Effective silvicultural operations play a crucial role in forest regeneration, especially with changing climate conditions (Routa et al., 2019; Achim et al., 2022).
However, the success of these operations depends on precise monitoring.
This includes assessing restoration success and optimizing interventions like planting, thinning and plant control.
An important challenge of this forest regeneration surveillance lies in the accurate identification of species composition, which is crucial for detecting competing vegetation, dead trees, and debris.
These components are essential for supporting informed and timely management decisions.
Traditionally, these data were gathered via ground-based surveys, but their time-intensive nature and the logistical challenges of accessing remote, rugged terrain make them inefficient for surveying large forest areas.
Consequently, alternative approaches have received increasing attention, as reflected in a recent survey of over 300 forest practitioners highlighting strong interest in species composition mapping using remote sensing for silvicultural planning (Fassnacht et al., 2025).

The transition to UAV imagery provides a highly scalable alternative for data collection, but it fundamentally shifts the bottleneck from physical field access to data interpretation.
Deep learning is a promising approach to the latter, but supervised learning algorithms require large quantities of precisely labelled data to generalize effectively across environments.
While the broader machine learning community has directed significant resources to create datasets toward mainstream perception tasks like urban autonomous driving or robotic grasping, fine-grained ecological perception remains an orphaned  Artificial Intelligence (AI) problem (Reynolds et al., 2025).
Thus, from a computer vision perspective, our species composition mapping represents a data-scarce problem.
Moreover, the task requires models to navigate widespread class imbalance, visual heterogeneity, and fuzzy boundaries, particularly at fine spatial scales such as small grass leaves.
Furthermore, unlike urban environments where bounding boxes are easily drawn by crowd-sourced workers, annotating high-resolution overhead images of vegetative cover requires specialized photo-interpretation by forestry or botanical experts, resulting in a severe scarcity of real annotated images.
Figure 2 presents on the left side an example of a UAV image and its corresponding expert annotation.
It highlights two problems: 1) expert annotations are generally approximations, and 2) the labelling process is time-consuming, as every pixel of the high-resolution image needs an annotation.

Previous approaches of doing photo-interpretation tasks on UAV imagery have focused more on mature forests, with a traditional supervised learning approach relying on hand-labelled images.
For instance, Detectree2 (Ball et al., 2023) was trained to perform tree crown segmentation in natural environments with 3.8k annotations, while BAMFORESTS (Troles et al., 2024) relied on 27k annotations.
Similar approaches have been done for tree species identification (Ferreira et al., 2020; Ecke et al., 2024).
In all cases, they required significant manual annotation efforts.
These limitations have increasingly motivated interest in alternative strategies that reduce reliance on exhaustively labelled real‑world imagery.
In parallel, one way to solve class imbalance in semantic segmentation, a key issue in our situation, is to perform random oversampling of minority classes.
However, this approach is ill-suited to images with strong intra-image class imbalance, such as vegetative cover scenes.
To mitigate this limitation, some alternative approaches exist, for instance, Soltani et al. (2025) present an automatic way of segmenting images of plants from one data source (citizen science data), and then pasting them into UAV imagery.
However, the quality of the augmentation is limited by the ability to segment the plant accurately, and then to harmonize its appearance with the target domain (UAV imagery).
An alternative approach to tackle both issues is the use of synthetic data (Grondin et al., 2023; Blaga and Nedevschi, 2026).
These efforts have historically relied on explicit procedural modelling using 3D assets and game engines, which struggle to accurately replicate the chaotic photorealism of the natural regeneration forests that define our operating environment.

In response to these considerations, we propose a comprehensive methodology that combines several techniques to address the lack of labelled data and class imbalance, depicted in Figure 1.
First, we make use of extremely small  Ground Sampling Distance (GSD), down to the millimetre-level.
As recently demonstrated by Soltani et al. (2024) and Nasiri et al. (2025), leveraging ultra-low-altitude UAV imagery captures intricate leaf structures comparable to citizen science images.
Such resolution effectively bridges the domain gap between aerial imagery and ground-level citizen science, enabling automated pseudo-labelling workflows that reduce the need for manual annotation.
To this effect, we introduce an extension of the WilDReF-Q dataset for species semantic segmentation in Quebec forest regeneration zones presented in (Nasiri et al., 2025), featuring 5050 new labelled images and 13 97713\,977 new unlabelled images taken in three bioclimatic domains in the province of Quebec.
Following Nasiri et al. (2025), we leverage citizen science data to produce pseudo-labels on the full unlabelled dataset.
Second, we explore the use of generative AI as a prompt-based training data generator.
Recent findings by Gabeur et al. (2026) demonstrate that large-scale image generation pre-training plays a foundational role analogous to large language model pre-training, equipping models such as Google’s Nano Banana Pro (Google, 2026) with deep, internalized representations of visual semantics and underlying geometric structures.
Incidentally, Zuo et al. (2025) also demonstrate Nano Banana Pro’s strong zero-shot capabilities for semantic tasks.
Consequently, we present a novel dataset called Gen4Regen, comprising 21012101 images and corresponding labels generated using the Nano Banana Pro model, as seen on the right side of Figure 2.
This approach allows practitioners in label-scarce domains, such as ours, to generate data for underrepresented classes under specific contexts via text prompts, further increasing domain diversity and improving generalization.
We also present actionable guidelines on harmonizing these generated image-mask pairs with real data to effectively mitigate the domain gap.
To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to demonstrate that large-scale image generators are now capable of conjointly synthesizing high-fidelity, photorealistic images alongside their precise semantic masks, in a single inference step.
Finally, as in Gabeur et al. (2026), we assess the potential of Nano Banana Pro as a zero-shot semantic segmentation for our task.

In short, our contributions are:

Gen4Regen, our novel synthetic dataset generated with Nano Banana Pro, containing 21012101 photorealistic images of forest regeneration environments and corresponding high-precision semantic segmentation masks;

An assessment of the potential of bootstrapping data-scarce, class-imbalanced projects such as ours, while improving geographical and environmental generalization;

WilDReF-Q-V2, an extension of the WilDReF-Q dataset with UAV images of natural forest regeneration vegetation, featuring 5050 new labelled images, 13 97713\,977 unlabelled images, an additional camera sensor, and improved annotations and folds;

An evaluation on the performance of zero-shot semantic segmentation for species composition mapping, with a large-scale AI generation model.

1. Gen4Regen, our novel synthetic dataset generated with Nano Banana Pro, containing 21012101 photorealistic images of forest regeneration environments and corresponding high-precision semantic segmentation masks;

2. An assessment of the potential of bootstrapping data-scarce, class-imbalanced projects such as ours, while improving geographical and environmental generalization;

3. WilDReF-Q-V2, an extension of the WilDReF-Q dataset with UAV images of natural forest regeneration vegetation, featuring 5050 new labelled images, 13 97713\,977 unlabelled images, an additional camera sensor, and improved annotations and folds;

4. An evaluation on the performance of zero-shot semantic segmentation for species composition mapping, with a large-scale AI generation model.
